title: Handling Events
description: Learn how to handle user interactions like clicks, input changes, and form submissions.

data.text: Events are actions that happen in the browser: clicks, key presses, form submissions, and more. React wraps native browser events in a cross-browser object called **SyntheticEvent** and uses camelCase names for handlers.
HTML uses lowercase event attributes. React uses camelCase because JSX is JavaScript. This is one of the first syntax differences beginners notice.
Pass a reference to a function — do not call the function inside the JSX attribute. Calling it immediately would run the handler during render instead of on the event.

data.title: Correct vs Incorrect

data.text: To pass arguments, wrap the call in an arrow function. This creates a new function that calls your handler with the desired arguments.

data.title: Passing Arguments
data.content: Sending an ID to a click handler

data.title: Arrow Function Shortcut
data.text: `onClick={() => handleClick(id)}` creates a new function on every render. For most cases this is fine. If performance becomes a concern, use useCallback to stabilize the reference.

Event handlers receive a **SyntheticEvent** object — React's wrapper around the native browser event. It gives you access to the target element, its value, and the ability to prevent default behavior.

data.text: Some browser actions — like form submission reloading the page — are unwanted in SPAs. Call `e.preventDefault()` to stop them.

items.question: Why does React use camelCase instead of lowercase?
items.answer: JSX is JavaScript, and JS keywords and DOM properties in JavaScript use camelCase (onclick becomes onClick).

items.question: Can I use the native event instead of SyntheticEvent?
items.answer: Yes. Access the native event via `e.nativeEvent`. Most code uses the SyntheticEvent because it normalizes behavior across browsers.

items.question: Do event handlers run in the same order as they are defined?
items.answer: Yes, for event bubbling. React attaches a single listener to the root and dispatches events internally.

items.question: Can I stop propagation in React?
items.answer: Yes. Use `e.stopPropagation()` to prevent the event from bubbling up to parent listeners.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: React events use camelCase: onClick, onChange, onSubmit.
Pass function references; do not call handlers in JSX attributes.
Use arrow functions to pass arguments to handlers.
Use e.preventDefault() to stop default browser behavior.
data.takeaway: Events connect user actions to state updates. Now that you know events and state, let's explore best practices for managing state effectively.
